Significant main effects of together/alone (F(1,396) = 4.44; p < 0.05) and trial-type (F(2,396) = 16.48; p < 0.05), as well as a significant interaction between self/other and trial-type (F(2,396) = 3.3; p < 0.05) were observed. Thus, rats froze more on shock trials when alone compared to when they were together.
claims.evidence: This is supported by ANOVA statistical analysis of freezing data.

claims.claim: Freezing was significantly stronger on self-shock trials when alone compared to when rats were together.
claims.source: Furthermore, post-hoc t tests demonstrate that freezing was significantly stronger on self-shock trials when alone compared to when rats were together (t(33) = 2.54; p < 0.05) and that freezing did not significantly differ on together-self-shock and together-other-shock trials (t(33) = 0.19; p = 0.85).
claims.evidence: This is supported by post-hoc t-test analysis of freezing data.

claims.claim: Freezing did not significantly differ on together-self-shock and together-other-shock trials.
claims.source: Furthermore, post-hoc t tests demonstrate that freezing was significantly stronger on self-shock trials when alone compared to when rats were together (t(33) = 2.54; p < 0.05) and that freezing did not significantly differ on together-self-shock and together-other-shock trials (t(33) = 0.19; p = 0.85).
claims.evidence: This is supported by post-hoc t-test analysis of freezing data.

claims.claim: Rats approached the conspecific's side of the box most often on together-shock-self trials.
claims.source: Rats approached the conspecific's side of the box most often on together-shock-self trials (Figure 3F; red).
claims.evidence: This is supported by video scoring data shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: Percent approach was significantly higher on together-shock trials compared to alone-shock-self and together-neutral-self trials for both 'self' and 'other' trial-types.
claims.source: For both 'self' and 'other' trial-types, percent approach was significantly higher on together-shock trials compared to alone-shock-self and together-neutral-self trials (Figure 3F and H; Wilcoxon; p's < 0.05).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of approach behavior shown in Figure 3F and H.

claims.claim: The recording rat approached the conspecific more during together-shock-self relative to together-shock-other trials.
claims.source: Although the recording rat approached the conspecific both during self and other shock trials, this effect was stronger when the threat was to the recording rat (together-shock-self versus together-shock-other; Figure 3F versus Figure 3H; red; Wilcoxon; p < 0.05).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of approach behavior shown in Figure 3F and H.

claims.claim: Approach was driven by the desire for social contact and shock, but only when the recording rat was threatened.
claims.source: These results suggest that approach was driven by the desire for social contact (i.e., more approach when the conspecific was present than when alone) and shock (i.e., more approach during shock trials than reward and neutral), but only when the recording rat was threatened (i.e., more approach during together-self-shock relative to together-shock-other trials).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the pattern of approach behavior across conditions.

claims.claim: When rats were alone, average DA release increased to cues that predicted reward-self trials significantly more than neutral trials.
claims.source: Consistent with this previous work, we found that when rats were alone, average DA release over all sessions (n = 40) increased to cues that predicted reward-self trials (blue) significantly more than neutral trials (green) during presentation of cues and reward (Figure 4A)
claims.evidence: This is supported by voltammetry data shown in Figure 4A and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: DA release was lower during presentation of cues that predicted unavoidable shock when rats were alone.
claims.source: and that DA release was lower during presentation of cues that predicted unavoidable shock (Figure 4A; red (shock) versus green (neutral) when alone (thin) during directional light cue presentations).
claims.evidence: This is supported by voltammetry data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The distributions of reward indices were significantly shifted in the positive direction indicating significantly higher DA release on reward trials relative to neutral trials during alone trials.
claims.source: The distributions of reward and shock indices were significantly shifted in the positive and negative direction indicating significantly higher (Figure 4F; Wilcoxon; µ = 24.6; p < 0.05) and lower (Figure 4G; Wilcoxon; µ = −11.5; p < 0.05) DA release on reward and shock trials relative to neutral trials, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of DA data shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: The distributions of shock indices were significantly shifted in the negative direction indicating significantly lower DA release on shock trials relative to neutral trials during alone trials.
claims.source: The distributions of reward and shock indices were significantly shifted in the positive and negative direction indicating significantly higher (Figure 4F; Wilcoxon; µ = 24.6; p < 0.05) and lower (Figure 4G; Wilcoxon; µ = −11.5; p < 0.05) DA release on reward and shock trials relative to neutral trials, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of DA data shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: The decline of DA release induced by the presentation of shock-self cues was attenuated in the presence of the conspecific.
claims.source: However, during shock-self trials, we found that the decline of DA release induced by the presentation of shock-self cues was attenuated in the presence of the conspecific (Figure 4A; thick versus thin red lines after outcome cue onset).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison of DA signals between alone and together conditions shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The distribution of 'shock minus neutral' indices calculated on shock-self trials were not significantly shifted when rats were together.
claims.source: Consistent with this observation, the distribution of 'shock minus neutral' indices calculated on shock-self trials were not significantly shifted (Figure 4I; Wilcoxon; µ = −1.4; p = 0.43) as they were during alone-shock-self trials (Figure 4G; Wilcoxon; µ = −11.5; p < 0.05).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of DA data shown in Figure 4I.

claims.claim: After the cue signaled a reward trial, there was an increase in DA release above neutral cues similar to what was observed during reward-self trials.
claims.source: After the cue signaled a reward trial, there was an increase in DA release above neutral cues similar to what was observed during reward-self trials (Wilcoxon; p < 0.05).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of DA data during reward-other trials.

claims.claim: Immediately after illumination of the directional light cue, DA release declined to pre-cue levels for both 'alone' and 'together' trials during reward-other trials.
claims.source: Only after directional cue presentation did rats become aware of who would receive the reward. In line with rats being self-interested, immediately after illumination of the directional light cue, DA release declined to pre-cue levels for both 'alone' and 'together' trials.
claims.evidence: This is supported by DA data during reward-other trials shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: DA release was significantly lower when reward was delivered to the conspecific compared to when reward was delivered to the recording rat.
claims.source: As a result, DA release was significantly lower when reward was delivered to the conspecific compared to when reward was delivered to the recording rat (Wilcoxon; p < 0.05).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of DA signals between reward-self and reward-other trials.

claims.claim: There were no significant differences in DA release between alone and together reward-other trials during the outcome epoch.
claims.source: This was true for both 'alone' and 'together' trials and there were no significant differences between them during the outcome epoch (Figure 5B; Wilcoxon; µ = −1.12; p = 0.86), which suggest that DA release during reward-other trials was not modulated by social context.
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of DA data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: DA release during reward-other trials was not modulated by social context.
claims.source: This was true for both 'alone' and 'together' trials and there were no significant differences between them during the outcome epoch (Figure 5B; Wilcoxon; µ = −1.12; p = 0.86), which suggest that DA release during reward-other trials was not modulated by social context.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the lack of difference between alone and together conditions.

claims.claim: Prior to shock delivery, DA release was similar during the outcome cue and directional cue epochs on shock-other trials.
claims.source: Although DA release on reward-other trials was not modulated by presence of the conspecific, shock-other trials were. Prior to shock delivery DA release was similar during the outcome cue and directional cue epochs (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by DA data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: DA release was not different on shock-other trials compared to together-shock-self trials.
claims.source: In fact, DA release was not different on shock-other trials compared to together-shock-self trials, reminiscent of the observation described above that rats froze at a similar level on together-shock-other compared to together-shock-self trials.
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison of DA signals across trial types.

claims.claim: There was no significant difference between together-self-shock and together-conspecific-shock trials in DA release during the directional cue epoch.
claims.source: Post-hoc t-tests yield a significant difference between alone-shock-self and together-shock-self (t(39) = 3.53; p < 0.05) consistent with the analysis described above, and no significant difference between together-self-shock and together-conspecific-shock trials (t(39) = 1.95; p = 0.06).
claims.evidence: This is supported by post-hoc t-test analysis of DA data.

claims.claim: After shock was delivered to the conspecific, DA release actually increased.
claims.source: Although prior to shock delivery, DA release was similar for together-shock-self, together-shock-other and alone-shock-other trials, we found that after shock was delivered to the conspecific, DA release actually increased (Figure 5A; thick red)
claims.evidence: This is supported by DA data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: DA release was significantly higher following shock delivery to the conspecific compared to neutral trials.
claims.source: DA release was significantly higher following shock delivery to the conspecific compared to neutral trials (Figure 5A; thick red versus thick green; Figure 5I; Wilcoxon; µ = 7.4; p < 0.05)
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of DA data shown in Figure 5I.

claims.claim: DA release was significantly higher following shock delivery to the conspecific compared to when shock was delivered to the conspecific's empty side of the cage.
claims.source: and compared to when shock was delivered to the conspecific's empty side of the cage (Figure 5A; thick red versus thin red; Figure 5D; Wilcoxon; µ = −8.6; p < 0.05).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of DA data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Rats took longer and were less likely to lever press on shock-other trials relative to non-shock trials.
claims.source: Over all recording sessions (n = 24), rats took longer (Figure 6F) and were less likely (Figure 1E) to lever press on shock-other trials relative to non-shock trials (Wilcoxon; p < 0.05) consistent with previous reports suggesting thats rat do perform 'prosocial' acts to benefit others in distress (Atsak et al., 2011; Ben-Ami Bartal et al., 2011; Ben-Ami Bartal et al., 2014; Burkett et al., 2016; Meyza et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6E and F and is consistent with previous literature.

claims.claim: Rats refrained from pressing significantly more often and were significantly slower when the auditory cues signaled shock to oneself as opposed to the conspecific.
claims.source: However, behavior was also strongly guided by individual outcomes rather than those of the conspecific. That is, rats refrained from pressing significantly more often and were significantly slower when the auditory cues signaled shock to oneself as opposed to the conspecific (Figure 6E and F; red vs orange; Wilcoxon; p's < 0.05).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 6E and F.

claims.claim: Rats approached the conspecific on 24% of footshock trials, but only following the lever press.
claims.source: On footshock trials, rats approached the conspecific on 24% of trials, but only following the lever press (Figure 6G; orange; 23% after lever press; 1% after no lever press; chi-square, p < 0.05).
claims.evidence: This is supported by video scoring data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 6G.

claims.claim: Rats occasionally approached the conspecific after the lever press on no-shock trials.
claims.source: Interestingly, rats also occasionally approached the conspecific after the lever press on no-shock trials (Figure 6G; blue; 13% after lever press; 1% after no lever press; chi-square, p < 0.05).
claims.evidence: This is supported by video scoring data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 6G.

claims.claim: Cues that predict avoidable shock increase DA release to a similar degree as cues that predict reward delivery.
claims.source: Although cues that predict unavoidable footshock suppress DA release (as in the Pavlovian Social Distress Paradigm described above; Figure 4), recent work has shown that cues that predict avoidable shock and avoidance of shock itself, DA release increases to a similar degree as to cues that predict reward delivery (Gentry et al., 2016; Oleson and Cheer, 2013; Oleson et al., 2012; Wenzel et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies and the current data.

claims.claim: DA release was observed on both reward and shock-self cues, with no difference between them.
claims.source: Figure 7 illustrates DA release over all recording sessions (n = 24) when rats pressed for reward (blue) and did not press to avoid self-shock (red). DA release was observed on both reward and shock-self cues, with no difference between them.
claims.evidence: This is supported by DA data shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: The distribution of differences between DA release on reward press and shock-self no press trials is not significantly shifted.
claims.source: This is quantified in Figure 7C, which plots the difference between DA release on reward press and shock-self no press trials (shock minus reward) for each session. The distribution is not significantly shifted indicating no differences between reward and shock-self trials (Wilcoxon; µ = −1.9; p = 0.95).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of DA data shown in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: A similar pattern of DA release emerged during shock-other no press trials as during non-press shock-self trials, but the magnitude of DA release was significantly lower on shock-other no press trials.
claims.source: Orange lines in Figure 7A represent shock-other trials when the recording rat did not press the lever for reward, thus avoiding shock for the conspecific. Remarkably a similar pattern of DA release emerged as during non-press shock-self trials, with DA release to the cue and during the absence of the shock; however, the magnitude of DA release was significantly lower on shock-other no press trials (orange) compared to when rats avoided self-shock (red) and when the rats pressed the lever on no-shock reward trials when there was no threat of shock (blue).
claims.evidence: This is supported by DA data shown in Figure 7A and statistical analysis.

claims.claim: DA release was significantly lower on shock-other trials relative to no-shock trials.
claims.source: This is quantified in Figure 7B and D, which plot the distributions of differences between shock-other and shock-self (shock-self minus shock-other), and between no-shock and shock-other trials (shock-other minus no-shock). Both distributions were significantly shifted (Wilcoxon; p's < 0.05; Figure 7B and D) indicating significantly lower DA release on shock-other trials relative to no-shock trials
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of DA data shown in Figure 7B and D.

claims.claim: DA release was significantly higher on shock-self relative to shock-other trials.
claims.source: This is quantified in Figure 7B and D, which plot the distributions of differences between shock-other and shock-self (shock-self minus shock-other), and between no-shock and shock-other trials (shock-other minus no-shock). Both distributions were significantly shifted (Wilcoxon; p's < 0.05; Figure 7B and D) indicating significantly lower DA release on shock-other trials relative to no-shock trials and significantly higher DA release on shock-self relative to shock-other trials.
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of DA data shown in Figure 7B and D.

claims.claim: Patients with psychopathic traits and autism have difficulties recognizing the mental states of others and appropriately altering behavior in social contexts.
claims.source: Importantly, patients with psychopathic traits and autism have difficulties recognizing the mental states of others and appropriately altering behavior in social contexts (Baron-Cohen et al., 1985; Blair, 2003; Buckholtz et al., 2010; Cook and Black, 2012; Gaigg, 2012; Hamilton, 2013; Matthys et al., 2013; Neuhaus et al., 2010; Rizzolatti and Fabbri-Destro, 2008; Scott-Van Zeeland et al., 2010; Taylor and DeQuinzio, 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by extensive citations to previous clinical literature.

claims.claim: These disorders are difficult to treat and currently lack effective pharmacological interventions.
claims.source: These disorders are difficult to treat and currently lack effective pharmacological interventions, reflecting the lack of knowledge pertaining to our understanding of the underlying neurobiology of how social cues may alter behavior.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about psychiatric disorders.

claims.claim: Rats will choose mutual reward in a prosocial task.
claims.source: For example, rats will choose mutual reward in a prosocial task, freeze when they see another rat freeze (interpreted as 'empathy') and exhibit 'prosocial' rescue behavior of a conspecific in distress.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on previous literature on rat social behavior.

claims.claim: Rats will rescue a conspecific that is confined in a restrainer, even when faced with a choice between freeing the trapped rat and obtaining food reward.
claims.source: Most notable was a recent set of high profile papers (Science; eLife) demonstrating that rats will rescue a conspecific that is confined in a restrainer, even when faced with a choice between freeing the trapped rat and obtaining food reward (Ben-Ami Bartal et al., 2011; Ben-Ami Bartal et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to specific high-profile studies.

claims.claim: Rats only freeze when they have experienced shock themselves.
claims.source: Although many of these studies are intriguing, they have met criticism; effects are often small, rats only freeze when they have experienced shock themselves, and rats do not free trapped conspecifics under all circumstances (Schwartz et al., 2017; Silberberg et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to critical literature.

claims.claim: Rats do not free trapped conspecifics under all circumstances.
claims.source: Although many of these studies are intriguing, they have met criticism; effects are often small, rats only freeze when they have experienced shock themselves, and rats do not free trapped conspecifics under all circumstances (Schwartz et al., 2017; Silberberg et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to critical literature.

claims.claim: 'Prosocial' rescue behavior might reflect some sort of reproductive benefit.
claims.source: Further, many of these effects are dependent on rats being cage mates or of the same strain, suggesting that 'prosocial' rescue behavior might reflect some sort of reproductive benefit.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on observed patterns in the literature.

claims.claim: Cues and outcomes directed to the conspecific did not produce the same pattern of DA results as those directed to the recording rat.
claims.source: Importantly, cues and outcomes directed to the conspecific did not produce the same pattern of results, suggesting that – if DA signals genuinely reflect value of predictive cues – cues that predicted conspecific reward and shock were not considered to be appetitive and aversive, respectively.
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison of DA signals between self and other trials.

claims.claim: Footshocks directed to the conspecific actually increased DA release.
claims.source: Moreover, footshocks directed to the conspecific actually increased DA release, suggesting that rats may have been using cues from conspecific (e.g., vocalizations, odors, visual, etc.) to determine that the shock had been delivered to the conspecific, signaling the value of personal safety or relief.
claims.evidence: This is supported by DA data during shock-other trials and is an interpretation of the signal.

claims.claim: The recording rat approached the other rat during the outcome, but did not freeze.
claims.source: This interpretation is supported by the freezing and approach behavior at the time of the shock. The rat that we recorded from approached the other rat during the outcome, but did not freeze.
claims.evidence: This is supported by video scoring data during shock-other trials.

claims.claim: The recording rat was engaged with the conspecific possibly to determine what will occur during the trial, but was not overly fearful during that period.
claims.source: This suggests that the recording rat was engaged with the conspecific possibly to determine what will occur during the trial, but was not overly fearful during that period (i.e., the period when DA increases during conspecific shock).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the pattern of approach and freezing behavior.

claims.claim: The presence of the other rat altered the subjective value placed on cues that predicted self-shock by reducing fear and the associated suppression of the DA signal during the Pavlovian paradigm.
claims.source: Remarkably, we also found that the presence of the other rat altered the subjective value placed on cues that predicted self-shock by reducing fear and the associated suppression of the DA signal during the Pavlovian paradigm.
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison of DA and behavioral data between alone and together conditions.

claims.claim: The recording rat approached the conspecific on shock-self trials, perhaps reflecting 'consolation' seeking behavior similar to what has been described in prairie voles.
claims.source: On these trials the rat approached the conspecific, perhaps reflecting 'consolation' seeking behavior similar to what has been described in prairie voles (Burkett et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on approach behavior and comparison to previous literature.

claims.claim: The lack of suppression of DA release during shock-self trials when together suggests that the recording rat found the shock cue to be subjectively less aversive in the presence of the conspecific.
claims.source: The lack of suppression of DA release during this period suggests that the recording rat found the shock cue to be subjectively less aversive in the presence of the conspecific.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on DA data during together-shock-self trials.

claims.claim: Rats entered the food cup and froze less often on together-shock-self trials.
claims.source: Indeed, rats entered the food cup and froze less often on together-shock-self trials.
claims.evidence: This is supported by behavioral data comparing alone and together shock-self trials.

claims.claim: In the instrumental task, rats pressed significantly less and were slower to press on conspecific-shock trials.
claims.source: In the context of the instrumental task rats pressed significantly less and were slower to press on conspecific-shock trials, demonstrating empathetic and prosocial behaviors consistent with previous reports (Atsak et al., 2011; Ben-Ami Bartal et al., 2011; Ben-Ami Bartal et al., 2014; Burkett et al., 2016; Meyza et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by behavioral data from the instrumental task and is consistent with previous literature.

claims.claim: DA release during decisions to give up reward and spare the conspecific from shock mirrored DA release when the rat avoided shock for itself.
claims.source: Remarkably, DA release during decisions to give up reward and spare the conspecific from shock mirrored DA release when the rat avoided shock for itself, suggesting that DA release during conspecific shock trials reflected the value of saving the conspecific similar to when it signals the value of saving oneself and that the same signal that encourages avoiding shock for oneself is present when avoiding shock for a conspecific.
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison of DA signals between shock-self and shock-other avoidance trials.

claims.claim: Lever pressing increased and DA release decreased during conspecific-shock compared to self-shock.
claims.source: However, lever pressing increased and DA release decreased during conspecific-shock compared to self-shock, which indicates that rats were more interested in sparing themselves from harm rather than sparing the conspecific.
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison of behavioral and DA data between shock-self and shock-other trials.

claims.claim: The DA signal is modulated by the degree of 'empathy' exhibited by rats in the context of this task.
claims.source: This suggests that the DA signal is modulated by the degree of 'empathy' exhibited by rats in the context of this task.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation based on the pattern of DA signals across conditions.

claims.claim: Rats do not always demonstrate 'empathetic' and 'prosocial' behavior as described previously or as expected in humans.

claims.claim: Each task structure promotes different levels of 'pro-social' and 'empathetic' behavior along a continuum.
claims.source: Importantly, across studies (ours and others) we don't think that these differences reflect problems with task design (ours or others), but that each task structure promotes different levels of 'pro-social' and 'empathetic' behavior along a continuum, providing insights into social behavior, and how the brain governs behavior and interprets outcomes in social contexts.

claims.claim: DA release is modulated by social context in at least three ways.
claims.source: For the first time, we show that DA release is modulated by social context in at least three ways.
claims.evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the three specific findings described next.

claims.claim: Reductions in DA release during cues that predict foot shock were weaker in the presence of the conspecific.
claims.source: First, reductions in DA release during cues that predict foot shock were weaker in the presence of the conspecific, likely due to comfort or distraction of being in the presence of another rat as evidenced by seeking social contact prior to and during foot shock delivery when together, but not alone.

claims.claim: DA release during shock trials increased when shock was administered to the conspecific.
claims.source: Second, DA release during shock trials increased when shock was administered to the conspecific, demonstrating that DA release was modulated by conspecific cues that indicated that the foot shock had occurred on the other side of the box.
claims.evidence: This is supported by DA data during shock-other trials.

claims.claim: During the instrumental task, cues that predict avoidable foot shock for the conspecific elicited a similar, but weaker DA release compared to cues that predicted avoidable foot shock for oneself.
claims.source: Third, during the instrumental task, cues that predict avoidable foot shock for the conspecific elicited a similar, but weaker DA release compared to cues that predicted avoidable foot shock for oneself.
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison of DA signals between shock-self and shock-other avoidance trials.

claims.claim: DA release is modulated by social context in that rats use social cues to optimize predictions about their own self-interest, even at the expense of a conspecific.
claims.source: Overall, we conclude that DA release is modulated by social context in that rats use social cues to optimize predictions about their own self-interest, even at the expense of a conspecific, and that correlates related to avoidance are present, albeit weaker, when consequences are directed to another rat as opposed to oneself.

results.result: The study used 34 male Sprague-Dawley rats in a modified shuttle box paradigm where pairs of rats were separated by a mesh divider allowing sensory contact. Eight rats underwent DA recording during the Pavlovian paradigm and nine during the instrumental task. Rats were individually housed, paired with the same conspecific throughout, and all procedures were IACUC-approved.
results.evaluation: Claims C23, C24, C99-C103 provide clear methodological details about subjects, housing, pairing, and ethical approval. These are straightforward descriptive claims about experimental design that are internally consistent and appropriately documented.

results.result: In the Pavlovian paradigm, rats correctly internalized auditory and directional cues, showing increased food cup entries on reward-self trials and decreased entries on shock-self trials relative to neutral trials. After directional cue presentation, food cup entries were significantly higher for reward-self compared to reward-other trials.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C29 are supported by behavioral data (beam breaks) shown in Figure 2A-B with appropriate statistical tests (Wilcoxon, p < 0.05). The pattern of responses demonstrates rats understood trial contingencies, which is essential for interpreting subsequent DA findings.

results.result: Social context modulated food cup approach behavior: rats visited the food cup significantly more on reward-other trials when alone (C30), and showed a trend toward reduced food cup suppression on shock-self trials when together with the conspecific (C31, p = 0.057).
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C31 are supported by statistical analysis of behavioral indices (Figure 2N, 2M). The near-significant result for C31 is appropriately reported with exact p-value. These findings suggest social presence reduces aversive responses to self-directed threats.

results.result: Freezing behavior was significantly elevated on shock-self trials compared to other trial types, both alone and together. Rats froze more on alone-shock-self trials than together-shock-self trials, but froze similarly on together-shock-self and together-shock-other trials. Rats did not show elevated freezing during shock-other trials compared to neutral-other trials.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C39 are supported by video scoring data with appropriate statistics (Wilcoxon tests, ANOVA, post-hoc t-tests; Figure 3A-D). The finding that rats freeze similarly to self-shock and conspecific-shock when together (C36, C39) is consistent with prior empathy literature, but the lack of freezing on shock-other vs. neutral-other trials (C34-C35) suggests context-dependent empathetic responses.

results.result: Rats approached the conspecific most often on together-shock-self trials, with approach significantly higher on shock trials compared to neutral trials for both self and other trial types. However, approach was stronger when the recording rat was threatened (shock-self) compared to when the conspecific was threatened (shock-other).
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C43 are supported by video scoring with statistical analysis (Figure 3F, 3H; Wilcoxon p < 0.05). The interpretation in C43 that approach reflects desire for social contact primarily when self-threatened is reasonable given the data pattern, though alternative explanations (e.g., information seeking) are not fully excluded.

results.result: When alone, DA release increased significantly to cues predicting reward-self trials and decreased to cues predicting shock-self trials, relative to neutral trials. These patterns replicate established findings about DA responses to appetitive and aversive predictive cues.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C47 are supported by voltammetry data (Figure 4A, 4F-G) with appropriate statistical tests (Wilcoxon, p < 0.05). These findings replicate well-established DA signaling patterns and serve as positive controls validating the recording methodology.

results.result: The presence of a conspecific attenuated the suppression of DA release normally induced by shock-self cues. When rats were together, the distribution of shock-minus-neutral indices was not significantly shifted, unlike when rats were alone.
results.evaluation: Claims C48, C49, and C3 are supported by comparison of DA signals between alone and together conditions (Figure 4A, 4I, 4D) with statistical analysis showing significant differences (Wilcoxon, p < 0.05 for alone-together comparison). This is a novel finding showing social buffering of aversive DA responses.

results.result: On reward-other trials, DA initially increased after the outcome cue (before rats knew who would receive reward), but declined to baseline after the directional cue revealed the conspecific would receive reward. DA release was significantly lower when reward was delivered to the conspecific compared to self, with no modulation by social context.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C56 are supported by DA data (Figure 5A-B) with statistical tests. The pattern suggests DA reflects subjective value (self-interest) rather than objective reward value. However, the interpretation that rats inferred non-receipt of reward (C53) is reasonable but not definitively proven—alternative explanations like attention shifts are possible.

results.result: Prior to shock delivery on shock-other trials, DA release was similar to together-shock-self trials. However, after shock was delivered to the conspecific, DA release actually increased, significantly higher than neutral trials and higher than when shock was delivered to the empty cage.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C62 and C5 are supported by DA data (Figure 5A, 5I, 5D) with statistical analysis (Wilcoxon, ANOVA, post-hoc tests). This counterintuitive finding—DA increase when conspecific is shocked—is well-documented but the interpretation (relief/safety signal) is inferential. The authors acknowledge ambiguity about whether this reflects self-safety vs. conspecific outcome.

results.result: In the instrumental task, rats took longer and were less likely to press on shock-other trials compared to no-shock trials, demonstrating prosocial behavior. However, rats refrained from pressing even more and were slower on shock-self trials compared to shock-other trials. Rats approached the conspecific after lever press on 24% of shock-other trials and 13% of no-shock trials.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C66 are supported by behavioral data (Figure 6E-G) with statistical analysis (Wilcoxon, chi-square, p < 0.05). The findings show both prosocial behavior (reduced pressing to spare conspecific) and self-interest (stronger avoidance of self-shock), providing behavioral context for DA findings.

results.result: Cues predicting avoidable shock (shock-self no-press trials) elicited DA release similar in magnitude to cues predicting reward (no-shock press trials), with no significant difference between them. This replicates prior findings that avoidable shock cues increase DA release.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C69 are supported by DA data (Figure 7, 7C) with statistical analysis (Wilcoxon, p = 0.95 for difference). This replicates established findings about DA responses to avoidable aversive outcomes and serves as a positive control for the instrumental paradigm.

results.result: DA release during shock-other no-press trials (when rats spared the conspecific) showed a similar pattern to shock-self no-press trials, but with significantly lower magnitude. DA release was significantly lower on shock-other trials compared to both no-shock trials and shock-self trials.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C72, C4, and C6 are supported by DA data (Figure 7A-D) with statistical analysis (Wilcoxon, p < 0.05). This key finding shows DA signals are present when sparing the conspecific but are attenuated compared to self-avoidance, supporting the subjective value interpretation.

results.result: DA release reflects subjective rather than objective evaluation of events occurring to another rat. DA signals were modulated by self-interest: cues predicting conspecific outcomes did not produce the same DA patterns as self-directed outcomes, DA increased when the conspecific (not self) was shocked, and DA release during conspecific avoidance was weaker than self-avoidance. The authors conclude DA is modulated by social context to optimize predictions about self-interest.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C12-C13, C80-C84, C86, C89-C91, C98 represent the central thesis supported by converging evidence from both paradigms. The subjective value interpretation is well-supported by the data patterns, though alternative interpretations (e.g., attention, salience) are not fully excluded. The interpretation that DA increase during conspecific shock reflects 'relief' (C81, C83) is reasonable but somewhat speculative—the authors acknowledge this ambiguity in the discussion.

results.result: Rats approached the conspecific and showed reduced freezing and food cup suppression on together-shock-self trials, interpreted as consolation-seeking behavior similar to prairie voles. This suggests the recording rat found shock cues subjectively less aversive in the conspecific's presence.
results.evaluation: Claims C85 and C87 are supported by behavioral data (approach, freezing, food cup entries), but the interpretation as 'consolation-seeking' is speculative. The comparison to prairie voles (C85) is cited but the behaviors differ (in voles, the non-distressed animal approaches the distressed one; here it's reversed). Alternative explanations like distraction or social buffering are equally plausible.

results.result: The authors conclude that rats do not always demonstrate empathetic and prosocial behavior as previously described or as expected in humans, and that different task structures promote different levels of prosocial behavior along a continuum.
results.evaluation: Claims C88, C92-C93 are interpretive conclusions supported by the mixed pattern of results showing both prosocial behaviors (reduced pressing to spare conspecific) and self-interested behaviors (stronger responses to self-directed outcomes). The continuum interpretation (C93) is reasonable but somewhat speculative—it's a framework for reconciling conflicting findings rather than a directly tested hypothesis.

results.result: DA release is modulated by social context in three ways: (1) reduced DA suppression to shock-self cues when together with conspecific, (2) increased DA when shock was delivered to conspecific, and (3) similar but weaker DA release when avoiding shock for conspecific vs. self.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C97 summarize the three main DA findings, each supported by the data from their respective claim groups. This is an appropriate high-level summary of the key empirical contributions.

results.result: The authors situate their work within the context of prior research on rat empathy and prosocial behavior, noting that while rats have been described as empathetic (freezing when others freeze, rescuing trapped conspecifics), these findings have met criticism and may be context-dependent. They also note the clinical relevance for understanding psychiatric disorders affecting social behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C7-C11, C73-C79 are background claims supported by extensive citations to prior literature. These appropriately contextualize the study and acknowledge both supportive and critical prior work. The citations appear appropriate though individual papers were not verified.

results.result: The authors review established knowledge about dopamine signaling, noting that DA is unique in signaling all aspects of reward prediction error, with DA increasing to better-than-expected events and decreasing to worse-than-expected events in both appetitive and aversive domains.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C22 are background claims about established DA function, supported by extensive citations to foundational literature. These claims provide necessary context for interpreting the novel findings. The characterization of DA as 'unique' (C14) in signaling all aspects of RPE is somewhat strong—other neuromodulators also show prediction error-like signals—but this is a minor issue in an otherwise accurate summary.
